ety.text: From Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μῑμικός (mīmikós, “belonging to mimes”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”); see mime.

senses.d: To imitate, especially in order to ridicule.
To take on the appearance of another, for protection or camouflage.
An entity that mimics another entity, such as a disease that resembles another disease in its signs and symptoms; see the great imitator.

ex: Jess jumped slightly at hearing Tillyʼs extremely accurate mimic of her voice.

senses.d: A fictional monster able to disguise itself as an inanimate object, commonly a treasure chest, often with the intent of luring adventurers into a trap.

ex: Oft, in her absence, mimic fancy wakes / To imitate her.

senses.d: Imitative; characterized by resemblance to other forms; applied to crystals which by twinning resemble simple forms of a higher grade of symmetry.
